state: Research scope: port only existing code under packages/, specifically packages/values exact arithmetic and wire/schema validation; supporting TypeScript adapters and Cloudflare binary delivery may change, compiler changes are outside scope. The compiler already uses Rust. Preserve current behavior rather than tighten APIs. Source facts checked on 2026-10-06: Decimal stores a coefficient limited to 38 decimal digits with scale 0..18, retaining trailing stored zeros; operators align scales, multiply exactly then round half-even, division uses minimal terminating scale or rounds to18, sum checks its final total to preserve order independence. Valid coefficients fit i128 but products need wider scratch. TS exported helpers accept arbitrary BigInt operands on some paths and check the result, so i64/i128 bindgen arguments would narrow too early. wasm-bindgen documents wrapping oversized BigInt. num-bigint provides arbitrary integers; bnum offers fixed-width types, and a 256-bit signed scratch suffices for valid binary Decimal operands, not arbitrary helper arguments without compatibility handling. rust_decimal uses a96-bit coefficient and cannot cover this decimal range. Existing tests include seeded Decimal.js cases and versioned wire/schema conformance, but no Wasm performance numbers. Schema validation performs normalization, trim, defaults on create only, omitted-update sentinels distinct from null, closed object checks, recursive mutation-version checks, secret wire refusal and ordered errors. Arbitrary input includes undefined and lone UTF16 surrogates; ordinary JSON/Rust String conversion may lose behavior. Locale/timezone/WHATWG URL remain host-mediated initially. A startup registry of normalized current descriptors can avoid repeated type grammar parsing for generated/registered types without compiler changes; arbitrary external invocation type strings retain compatibility validation. One shared Rust core and a Wasm adapter keep the same synchronous TS façade; semantic parity precedes deployment, and native NAPI plus fixed-width optimization can be later work. No measured speedup or Rust prototype is claimed.

arithmetic_backend.instructions: Which first Rust arithmetic backend best preserves the inspected package API with reviewable implementation and a credible route to later optimization? Compare full parity, proof effort, dependencies and maintenance without assuming speed gains.

criteria.bigint_first: Implement Can's own coefficient/scale and error rules on num-bigint first, preserving arbitrary helper arguments and wide intermediates. Use existing differential tests, then consider fixed width after bounds proofs and measurements. Costs: heap allocation and larger Wasm/dependency footprint can erase speed benefits, requiring another optimization step.
criteria.fixed_first: Use bounded i128 values and bnum I256 scratch immediately for admitted operands, plus an explicit arbitrary-BigInt compatibility path for exported helpers. Prove every aggregate/intermediate bound and test both routes. Costs: more code, proofs and two routes from the start; benefit: predictable fixed-width storage and potential allocation savings, still unmeasured.
criteria.decimal_wrapper: Wrap bigdecimal with explicit Can scale/range/error/rounding constraints and custom compatibility conversions. Reuse its arbitrary-size decimal representation and operations where matched. Costs: audit library precision/rounding and canonicalization carefully and override divergent behavior; benefit: less handwritten division machinery.

validator_backend.instructions: Which package-only Rust validation strategy most simply preserves complete existing outputs, omissions and ordered errors while removing repeated parsing of registered types?

criteria.can_interpreter: Normalize current descriptors once into an ordered typed Can validation plan, register it in Rust, and interpret that plan with explicit Can rules. Keep a compatibility parser for genuinely dynamic IDs and JS adaptation for host behavior. Costs: custom semantic traversal and lossless boundary work; benefit: direct control of Can construction and error ordering.
criteria.json_schema: Compile generic JSON Schema validators in Rust and surround them with Can custom keywords/preprocessing/postprocessing, typed construction and error translation. Costs: dependency size and complex parity glue; benefit: mature reusable schema machinery and external-schema interoperability.
criteria.hybrid: Retain authoritative schema traversal in TypeScript, calling Rust for exact scalar parsing/arithmetic and selected leaf predicates. Costs: split ownership and possibly many JS/Wasm crossings; benefit: lower initial omission/error-order migration risk and simpler incremental rollout.
